open-question.question: What function-derived subject does the bootstrap commit carry, given it has no milestone id to serve as descriptor (a marker such as Workflow-bootstrap: with what descriptor), and is the commit subject-only like the other setup skills or does it carry a body naming which files were created versus preserved?

Does the git work-tree check run before or after the Python check, does a project failing both get one combined stop message or two separate stops on successive runs, and does the git check run on every invocation including a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project, as the Python check does?
open-question.alternative: Keep step 1 as it is and add the git work-tree check as a new step right after it, before state detection. Both checks run on every invocation. Each check stops on its own with its own message, so a project that fails both is stopped by the Python check first and hears about git only on the next run. It extends the existing step 1 template without changing it. Each stop keeps its single four-part message unchanged, the Python check's wording and position stay as they are, and a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project gets both checks the same way. A project missing both prerequisites needs two failed runs before it learns everything it must fix. The order puts the rarer failure (no suitable python3) ahead of the one a fresh empty directory is most likely to hit (not a git repository).

Put the git work-tree check first, ahead of the Python check, with both still running on every invocation before state detection. Each check stops on its own with its own message, so a project that fails both learns about git first and about Python on the next run. The failure most likely in a fresh directory is reported first, and it has the cheapest remedy (git init). Commit capability is also the more basic requirement, because every committing skill needs it while only the question skills need python3. Each stop still keeps its own single four-part message. Step 1 is renumbered and the Python check is no longer the opening check the skill's opening paragraph describes, so the prose and docs/skill-reference.md that present the Python check as the first thing the skill does need edits. A project failing both still needs two runs.

Run both checks on every invocation before state detection, always evaluating both, and stop once with a single message when either fails. The message covers each failing prerequisite in the four-part shape (what it looked for, what it found, the remedy) and ends with one closing line saying that a re-run completes the bootstrap. A project failing both prerequisites learns everything it must fix in one run. The order question goes away except as the order of sections in the message, which matters most for first-time users bootstrapping an empty directory. Step 1's one-check, one-message template has to be restructured into a collect-then-report step, so the Python check's stop logic and message are rewritten rather than left alone. The stop message is longer and has more branches, and how it is laid out depends on how the sibling question about git-check remedy wording settles the git message's shape.

Keep the Python check first and on every invocation. Run the git work-tree check after state detection and only on the path that will write, so a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project stops as "already initialized" without checking for git. The check is required only where it matters. A no-op re-run writes nothing and commits nothing, so it has no need for a git repository, and the scaffolding step's precondition stays next to the commit it protects. It departs from the Python check's every-invocation rule, so the two prerequisites behave differently. A re-run would no longer serve as a health check: an already-bootstrapped project that is not a git repository gets told it is initialized, and then every later committing skill fails at the commit procedure, which assumes a work tree and checks for none.

open-question.question: When the project is not a git repository, does the stop message tell the user to run git init and re-run, or does the skill offer to initialize the repository itself, and does the message follow the four-part shape of the Python stop message (what it looked for, what it found, the remedy, that a re-run completes the bootstrap)?

When CLAUDE.md or milestones/README.md already carries uncommitted changes before the bootstrap runs (for example a CLAUDE.md just written by /init and never committed), does the bootstrap's path-scoped commit sweep those unrelated hunks into its own commit, stop before writing, or proceed and note it?

Does the bootstrap's step 6 report become the one fixed identifier-free status line the other committing skills print, with a distinct line for the already-initialized no-op path, and does the suggestion to run /init and /define-milestone-goal next survive as an advisory or get cut along with the created-versus-preserved itemization?

Beyond the three places the goal names, are the CLAUDE.md pipeline listing that tags the skill non-committing, design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence, and the README's "one runtime prerequisite" sentence with its two host copies under scripts/hosts also updated to record git as a second prerequisite and the bootstrap as committing?

Should docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md gain a chain that starts from an empty repository with the bootstrap line, now that the bootstrap commits and a headless chain can include it without leaving files behind, or do the chains keep assuming an already-bootstrapped repository?

Does the git prerequisite pass whenever the workspace root is inside any git work tree (for example a subdirectory of a larger repository), or only when the workspace root is itself the repository's top level, and does a freshly initialized repository with no commits yet pass?
